## Best-Fit Native Tree Species for EBTL and Expected First-Year Survival

### Site context

**Elephants by the Lake (EBTL)** is a ~70-acre forest restoration project at **Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu**, in the foothills of the Eastern Ghats. The target ecosystem is the **South Deccan Plateau dry deciduous forest** (WWF ecoregion IM0202) — a critically endangered biome in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats, receiving 900–1,500 mm of monsoon rainfall (Jun–Sep), with hot, dry summers (Mar–May) when canopy trees are leafless. The site is degraded former forest on red/laterite soils adjoining remnant hill forest. EBTL's nursery (operated with Team Ananas) focuses on native flora of this ecoregion and had ~100+ native species in production as of 2023.

### Method

I identified candidate species by triangulating three independent lines of evidence:

1. **Ecoregion reference flora** — the characteristic species of the South Deccan Plateau dry deciduous forest biome (Wikipedia/One Earth ecoregion profiles, citing Champion & Seth's forest type classification).
2. **Local field inventories** — quantitative vegetation surveys in Krishnagiri/Dharmapuri districts and the adjacent Southern Eastern Ghats, ranked by Importance Value Index (IVI):
   - Ravi et al. (2024), "Diversity and Economic Value Trees in Krishnagiri Taluk" — 115 species recorded.
   - Sundarapandian & Swamy (2013), tree inventory of Tiruvannamalai (Sathanur RF) — *Albizia amara* dominant, *Chloroxylon swietenia* co-dominant.
   - Pragasan & Parthasarathy (2010), "Floristic Diversity … Dharmapuri Forest Division" — *Albizia amara*, *Anogeissus latifolia*, *Chloroxylon swietenia* among top IVI species.
   - Naidu & Kumar (2016), Southern Eastern Ghats disturbance gradient — *Pterocarpus santalinus*, *Anogeissus latifolia*, *Chloroxylon swietenia* predominant.
3. **Restoration trial results from comparable Eastern Ghats sites** — Ramachandran & Radhapriya (2016), Nanmangalam RF restoration trial with 12 native species over 1,080 days.

Species were ranked "best fit" if they: (a) appear in the reference flora *and* local inventories with high IVI, (b) have demonstrated restoration performance in comparable sites, and (c) span multiple ecological guilds (pioneer, mid-successional, climax) and canopy layers needed for structural complexity.

### Recommended species

| Species | Common name | Guild / role | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Albizia amara** | Oil-cake tree | Pioneer canopy (N-fixer) | Dominant by IVI at Sathanur & Dharmapuri; ecoregion characteristic |
| **Anogeissus latifolia** | Axlewood / Dhawda | Mid-successional canopy | Top-3 IVI across all Eastern Ghats surveys; fire-resistant bark |
| **Chloroxylon swietenia** | Satin wood | Mid-successional canopy | Co-dominant at Sathanur; characteristic ecoregion species |
| **Terminalia bellirica** | Baheda | Mid-successional canopy | Ecoregion characteristic; strong performer in Nanmangalam trial |
| **Terminalia elliptica** (syn. *T. alata*) | Marudha maram | Upper canopy, climax | High IVI across surveys; large-stature canopy scaffold |
| **Wrightia tinctoria** | Pala indigo | Understorey/mid-canopy | Good growth in Nanmangalam trial; frequent in Dharmapuri inventories |
| **Diospyros montana** | Bombay ebony | Understorey | Ecoregion characteristic; common in local surveys |
| **Pterocarpus marsupium** | Indian kino | Upper canopy (legume) | Ecoregion characteristic; high-value climax species |
| **Cassia fistula** | Golden shower | Pioneer/mid-canopy | Common across all inventory sites; fast establishment |
| **Pongamia pinnata** | Indian beech | Pioneer (N-fixer, riparian) | Best biomass performer in Nanmangalam restoration trial |
| **Dalbergia latifolia** | Indian rosewood | Climax canopy (legume) | Ecoregion characteristic; recorded in Krishnagiri inventories |
| **Hardwickia binata** | Anjan | Climax canopy (legume) | Ecoregion characteristic; slow-growing but key structural species |
| **Syzygium cumini** | Jamun | Mid-canopy (riparian/mesic) | Strong performer in Nanmangalam trial; good near water features |
| **Boswellia serrata** | Indian frankincense | Mid-canopy, dry-site specialist | Ecoregion characteristic; good on rocky/thin soils |
| **Tamarindus indica** | Tamarind | Canopy (legume) | Strong performer in Nanmangalam trial; local livelihood value |

**Supporting species** worth including in lower numbers: *Shorea talura*, *Strychnos nux-vomica*, *Holoptelea integrifolia*, *Phyllanthus emblica* (amla), *Premna tomentosa*, *Vitex altissima*, *Santalum album* (if host trees are established first), *Albizia lebbeck*, *Azadirachta indica* (neem), and *Gmelina arborea*.

### Expected first-year survival

The best available benchmark is the pan-Asian meta-analysis by **Banin et al. (2023)**, published in *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B* (378: 20210090). Key findings from 176 restoration sites (221,199 planted trees):

| Time since planting | Mean mortality | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| 1 year | **18.0%** | 14.5–22.2% |
| 2 years | 25.8% | 20.1–32.7% |
| 5–10 years | 44.0% | 39.5–48.7% |

**This translates to ~82% mean first-year survival** (95% CI: 78–86%).

However, the study found **mortality ~20% higher in open/deforested areas** compared to degraded-forest enrichment planting. Since EBTL's outplanting areas are largely open, degraded foothill valley (not forest enrichment), the site-adjusted expectation is:

> **First-year survival: approximately 60–80%** (i.e., 20–40% mortality), depending on management intensity.

Key modifiers at EBTL specifically:

- **Upside factors**: active nursery with hardened seedlings, permaculture soil-building (compost, mulch), community workforce for maintenance, proximity to remnant hill forest (seed rain, mycorrhizal inoculum), and focused native species selection.
- **Downside factors**: severe dry season (Mar–May), livestock browsing risk, degraded/thin soils in the valley, potential elephant trampling.
- **Species-specific variation**: Pioneers like *Albizia amara*, *Cassia fistula*, and *Pongamia pinnata* will likely exceed 80% first-year survival. Slower climax species like *Hardwickia binata*, *Dalbergia latifolia*, and *Pterocarpus marsupium* may show 50–70% without protection and supplemental irrigation through the first dry season.

The Nanmangalam RF trial (Ramachandran & Radhapriya, 2016) in comparable Eastern Ghats conditions showed **all 12 native species survived the 1,080-day trial period** with PGPB inoculation and minimal compost — but this was a managed research plot, so it represents an upper bound.

### Practical recommendations

1. **Plant a mix of guilds**: ~40% N-fixing pioneers (*Albizia amara*, *Pongamia pinnata*, *Albizia lebbeck*), ~40% mid-successional (*Anogeissus*, *Chloroxylon*, *Terminalia* spp., *Wrightia*), ~20% climax species (*Pterocarpus*, *Dalbergia*, *Hardwickia*).
2. **Time planting to early monsoon** (June–July) to maximize the first wet-season root establishment window.
3. **Protect outplants** from browsing in year 1 (tree guards or fencing) — this is the single largest controllable mortality factor.
4. **Supplemental watering** through the first dry season (Mar–May) will substantially improve survival of climax species.
5. **Budget for 20–30% infill replanting** in year 2.

### Key citations

- Banin, L.F. et al. (2023). "The road to recovery: a synthesis of outcomes from ecosystem restoration in tropical and sub-tropical Asian forests." *Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B* 378: 20210090. [doi:10.1098/rstb.2021.0090](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2021.0090)
- Ramachandran, A. & Radhapriya, P. (2016). "Restoration of Degraded Soil in the Nanmangalam Reserve Forest with Native Tree Species." *The Scientific World Journal* 2016: 5465841. [doi:10.1155/2016/5465841](https://doi.org/10.1155/2016/5465841)
- Sundarapandian, S. & Swamy, P.S. (2013). "Inventory of trees in tropical dry deciduous forests of Tiruvannamalai district, Tamil Nadu." *Biodiversitas* 15(2). [doi:10.13057/biodiv/d150208](https://doi.org/10.13057/biodiv/d150208)
- Pragasan, L.A. & Parthasarathy, N. (2010). "Floristic Diversity, Vegetation Analysis and Threat Status of Plants in Dharmapuri Forest Division." *Not. Bot. Horti Agrobot.* 10(2). [doi:10.15835/nsb10210158](https://doi.org/10.15835/nsb10210158)
- Naidu, M.T. & Kumar, O.A. (2016). "Assessment of Tree Population Structure and Diversity Along Disturbance Gradient in Tropical Dry Deciduous Forests, Southern Eastern Ghats." *Environment and Ecology* 42(3).
- Ravi, V. et al. (2024). "Diversity and Economic Value Trees in Krishnagiri Taluk, Tamil Nadu." *Indian J. Ecology* 51(3). [doi:10.55362/ije/2024/4303](https://doi.org/10.55362/ije/2024/4303)
- Wikipedia / One Earth, "South Deccan Plateau dry deciduous forests" (ecoregion IM0202), based on Champion & Seth (1968) forest-type classification.

### Caveats

- EBTL does not publish a full species list or survival monitoring data publicly. The recommendations above are derived from the regional ecology literature, not from EBTL's own records.
- The Banin et al. meta-analysis covers all of tropical/subtropical Asia, not specifically Indian dry deciduous sites. The 18% year-1 mortality figure is a pan-Asian mean; Indian dry deciduous sites may skew higher due to the severity of the dry season.
- Actual survival is heavily site-specific. EBTL should track its own cohort survival data (which its Centre for Eastern Ghats Studies likely does) and adjust species mixes accordingly.

Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) - A forest restoration project in the Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu

Over decades, the dry deciduous forests of our country have been stripped and exploited for commercial use. As native forests receded to only higher elevations of hills, creatures of the forests have also lost their footing in the valley. EBTL lies in one of those valleys. In the foothills of a degraded forest.

These 70 acres now 'belong' to us. How wonderful would it be if the other creatures also echoed the same thought? Our goal is to help the forest regain its rich biodiversity.

The year we began work, a few elephants came to the land, something that had never happened in the last many decades. We decided to call this project.

# Elephants By The Lake!

# The map of EBTL

Once you step into the hills around EBTL there are remnants of a once thriving forest; bird calls, fresh bear tracks, the jumping away of a troupe of langurs, trees in bloom or seed, spiders waiting for a catch, the scuffling across of a monitor lizard, a bird of prey gliding above.

Unfortunately this biodiverse ecosystem of the Eastern Ghats has been almost eradicated in terms of its area, but for a few hilly pockets where the tough terrain has made it too difficult for people to interfere.

Hopefully in time, the land will begin a cycle of regeneration where at a point, this space can become a safe corner for some of the rarer and threatened flora of the Eastern Ghats to flourish and wildlife can reinhabit the land.

# What happens at EBTL

#### Forest restoration

EBTL, primarily is focused on the native flora of the dry decidious forests of the South Deccan plateau.

#### Centre for Eastern Ghats Studies

We have established a dedicated in-house field research initiative at our campus in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu, to address critical gaps in knowledge about Eastern Ghats biodiversity, ecology, and conservation priorities.

#### Organic farming

A small percentage of land we own is allotted for farming where we grow paddy, pulses, millets and vegetables.

#### Farmer's Collective

We work very closely with the nearby village of Chinnathamandrapalli. The villagers play a vital role in all the work we undertake. We have enabled a collective of women working towards value added products. They also manage our farm lands and campus.

# Farmer's Collective

We promote land stewardship and sustainable farming by employing the local community and supporting a farmers collective to create value-added products. Our goal is to provide eco-friendly job opportunities to counter urban migration among the younger generation.

## Best-Fit Native Tree Species for EBTL and Expected First-Year Survival

### Site context

**Elephants by the Lake (EBTL)** is a ~70-acre forest restoration project at **Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu**, in the foothills of the Eastern Ghats. The target ecosystem is the **South Deccan Plateau dry deciduous forest** (WWF ecoregion IM0202) — a critically endangered biome in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats, receiving 900–1,500 mm of monsoon rainfall (Jun–Sep), with hot, dry summers (Mar–May) when canopy trees are leafless. The site is degraded former forest on red/laterite soils adjoining remnant hill forest. EBTL's nursery (operated with Team Ananas) focuses on native flora of this ecoregion and had ~100+ native species in production as of 2023.

### Method

I identified candidate species by triangulating three independent lines of evidence:

1. **Ecoregion reference flora** — the characteristic species of the South Deccan Plateau dry deciduous forest biome (Wikipedia/One Earth ecoregion profiles, citing Champion & Seth's forest type classification).
2. **Local field inventories** — quantitative vegetation surveys in Krishnagiri/Dharmapuri districts and the adjacent Southern Eastern Ghats, ranked by Importance Value Index (IVI):
   - Ravi et al. (2024), "Diversity and Economic Value Trees in Krishnagiri Taluk" — 115 species recorded.
   - Sundarapandian & Swamy (2013), tree inventory of Tiruvannamalai (Sathanur RF) — *Albizia amara* dominant, *Chloroxylon swietenia* co-dominant.
   - Pragasan & Parthasarathy (2010), "Floristic Diversity … Dharmapuri Forest Division" — *Albizia amara*, *Anogeissus latifolia*, *Chloroxylon swietenia* among top IVI species.
   - Naidu & Kumar (2016), Southern Eastern Ghats disturbance gradient — *Pterocarpus santalinus*, *Anogeissus latifolia*, *Chloroxylon swietenia* predominant.
3. **Restoration trial results from comparable Eastern Ghats sites** — Ramachandran & Radhapriya (2016), Nanmangalam RF restoration trial with 12 native species over 1,080 days.

Species were ranked "best fit" if they: (a) appear in the reference flora *and* local inventories with high IVI, (b) have demonstrated restoration performance in comparable sites, and (c) span multiple ecological guilds (pioneer, mid-successional, climax) and canopy layers needed for structural complexity.

### Recommended species

| Species | Common name | Guild / role | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Albizia amara** | Oil-cake tree | Pioneer canopy (N-fixer) | Dominant by IVI at Sathanur & Dharmapuri; ecoregion characteristic |
| **Anogeissus latifolia** | Axlewood / Dhawda | Mid-successional canopy | Top-3 IVI across all Eastern Ghats surveys; fire-resistant bark |
| **Chloroxylon swietenia** | Satin wood | Mid-successional canopy | Co-dominant at Sathanur; characteristic ecoregion species |
| **Terminalia bellirica** | Baheda | Mid-successional canopy | Ecoregion characteristic; strong performer in Nanmangalam trial |
| **Terminalia elliptica** (syn. *T. alata*) | Marudha maram | Upper canopy, climax | High IVI across surveys; large-stature canopy scaffold |
| **Wrightia tinctoria** | Pala indigo | Understorey/mid-canopy | Good growth in Nanmangalam trial; frequent in Dharmapuri inventories |
| **Diospyros montana** | Bombay ebony | Understorey | Ecoregion characteristic; common in local surveys |
| **Pterocarpus marsupium** | Indian kino | Upper canopy (legume) | Ecoregion characteristic; high-value climax species |
| **Cassia fistula** | Golden shower | Pioneer/mid-canopy | Common across all inventory sites; fast establishment |
| **Pongamia pinnata** | Indian beech | Pioneer (N-fixer, riparian) | Best biomass performer in Nanmangalam restoration trial |
| **Dalbergia latifolia** | Indian rosewood | Climax canopy (legume) | Ecoregion characteristic; recorded in Krishnagiri inventories |
| **Hardwickia binata** | Anjan | Climax canopy (legume) | Ecoregion characteristic; slow-growing but key structural species |
| **Syzygium cumini** | Jamun | Mid-canopy (riparian/mesic) | Strong performer in Nanmangalam trial; good near water features |
| **Boswellia serrata** | Indian frankincense | Mid-canopy, dry-site specialist | Ecoregion characteristic; good on rocky/thin soils |
| **Tamarindus indica** | Tamarind | Canopy (legume) | Strong performer in Nanmangalam trial; local livelihood value |

**Supporting species** worth including in lower numbers: *Shorea talura*, *Strychnos nux-vomica*, *Holoptelea integrifolia*, *Phyllanthus emblica* (amla), *Premna tomentosa*, *Vitex altissima*, *Santalum album* (if host trees are established first), *Albizia lebbeck*, *Azadirachta indica* (neem), and *Gmelina arborea*.

### Expected first-year survival

The best available benchmark is the pan-Asian meta-analysis by **Banin et al. (2023)**, published in *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B* (378: 20210090). Key findings from 176 restoration sites (221,199 planted trees):

| Time since planting | Mean mortality | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| 1 year | **18.0%** | 14.5–22.2% |
| 2 years | 25.8% | 20.1–32.7% |
| 5–10 years | 44.0% | 39.5–48.7% |

**This translates to ~82% mean first-year survival** (95% CI: 78–86%).

However, the study found **mortality ~20% higher in open/deforested areas** compared to degraded-forest enrichment planting. Since EBTL's outplanting areas are largely open, degraded foothill valley (not forest enrichment), the site-adjusted expectation is:

> **First-year survival: approximately 60–80%** (i.e., 20–40% mortality), depending on management intensity.

Key modifiers at EBTL specifically:

- **Upside factors**: active nursery with hardened seedlings, permaculture soil-building (compost, mulch), community workforce for maintenance, proximity to remnant hill forest (seed rain, mycorrhizal inoculum), and focused native species selection.
- **Downside factors**: severe dry season (Mar–May), livestock browsing risk, degraded/thin soils in the valley, potential elephant trampling.
- **Species-specific variation**: Pioneers like *Albizia amara*, *Cassia fistula*, and *Pongamia pinnata* will likely exceed 80% first-year survival. Slower climax species like *Hardwickia binata*, *Dalbergia latifolia*, and *Pterocarpus marsupium* may show 50–70% without protection and supplemental irrigation through the first dry season.

The Nanmangalam RF trial (Ramachandran & Radhapriya, 2016) in comparable Eastern Ghats conditions showed **all 12 native species survived the 1,080-day trial period** with PGPB inoculation and minimal compost — but this was a managed research plot, so it represents an upper bound.

### Practical recommendations

1. **Plant a mix of guilds**: ~40% N-fixing pioneers (*Albizia amara*, *Pongamia pinnata*, *Albizia lebbeck*), ~40% mid-successional (*Anogeissus*, *Chloroxylon*, *Terminalia* spp., *Wrightia*), ~20% climax species (*Pterocarpus*, *Dalbergia*, *Hardwickia*).
2. **Time planting to early monsoon** (June–July) to maximize the first wet-season root establishment window.
3. **Protect outplants** from browsing in year 1 (tree guards or fencing) — this is the single largest controllable mortality factor.
4. **Supplemental watering** through the first dry season (Mar–May) will substantially improve survival of climax species.
5. **Budget for 20–30% infill replanting** in year 2.

### Key citations

- Banin, L.F. et al. (2023). "The road to recovery: a synthesis of outcomes from ecosystem restoration in tropical and sub-tropical Asian forests." *Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B* 378: 20210090. [doi:10.1098/rstb.2021.0090](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2021.0090)
- Ramachandran, A. & Radhapriya, P. (2016). "Restoration of Degraded Soil in the Nanmangalam Reserve Forest with Native Tree Species." *The Scientific World Journal* 2016: 5465841. [doi:10.1155/2016/5465841](https://doi.org/10.1155/2016/5465841)
- Sundarapandian, S. & Swamy, P.S. (2013). "Inventory of trees in tropical dry deciduous forests of Tiruvannamalai district, Tamil Nadu." *Biodiversitas* 15(2). [doi:10.13057/biodiv/d150208](https://doi.org/10.13057/biodiv/d150208)
- Pragasan, L.A. & Parthasarathy, N. (2010). "Floristic Diversity, Vegetation Analysis and Threat Status of Plants in Dharmapuri Forest Division." *Not. Bot. Horti Agrobot.* 10(2). [doi:10.15835/nsb10210158](https://doi.org/10.15835/nsb10210158)
- Naidu, M.T. & Kumar, O.A. (2016). "Assessment of Tree Population Structure and Diversity Along Disturbance Gradient in Tropical Dry Deciduous Forests, Southern Eastern Ghats." *Environment and Ecology* 42(3).
- Ravi, V. et al. (2024). "Diversity and Economic Value Trees in Krishnagiri Taluk, Tamil Nadu." *Indian J. Ecology* 51(3). [doi:10.55362/ije/2024/4303](https://doi.org/10.55362/ije/2024/4303)
- Wikipedia / One Earth, "South Deccan Plateau dry deciduous forests" (ecoregion IM0202), based on Champion & Seth (1968) forest-type classification.

### Caveats

- EBTL does not publish a full species list or survival monitoring data publicly. The recommendations above are derived from the regional ecology literature, not from EBTL's own records.
- The Banin et al. meta-analysis covers all of tropical/subtropical Asia, not specifically Indian dry deciduous sites. The 18% year-1 mortality figure is a pan-Asian mean; Indian dry deciduous sites may skew higher due to the severity of the dry season.
- Actual survival is heavily site-specific. EBTL should track its own cohort survival data (which its Centre for Eastern Ghats Studies likely does) and adjust species mixes accordingly.
